title: Greet Phoebe (Romans 16)
hook: the letter ends with a list of people, many of them women, like Phoebe the deacon

segments.voice: Yesterday, proslambanesthe: the weak and the strong at one table. Your line was welcome one another.

Chapter sixteen of Romans looks like the credits at the end of a movie: a long list of names nobody can pronounce. Greet this one. Greet that one. Salute the household of so-and-so. Most people skip it. But stay for the credits: some of the best stories in the letter hide in that list. The very first name belongs to a woman traveling from a port town near Corinth, probably with the letter itself in her bag.
screen: `THE CREDITS AT THE END.` → `A LIST NOBODY READS.` → `THE FIRST NAME: A WOMAN WITH THE LETTER.`

segments.voice: Paul writes, in the King James Bible: "I commend unto you Phebe our sister, which is a servant of the church which is at Cenchrea." Cenchreae was the eastern port of Corinth. Servant here is diakonos, the root of deacon. Paul uses the same word for himself as a minister of the gospel, and even for Christ. Many scholars think Phoebe carried this letter to Rome, so she may have been the first to read it aloud there and answer questions about it. Paul asks the Romans to help her in whatever she needs, and calls her a helper, a patron, of many, and of Paul himself. Then the list. Priscilla and Aquila, a wife and husband who, Paul says, risked their necks for him, and who host a church in their home. Mary, who worked hard. Andronicus and Junia, who were in prison with Paul, and whom he calls of note among the apostles. Tryphaena and Tryphosa, two women who labor in the Lord. Rufus's mother, who, Paul says, was a mother to him too. More than two dozen names, around a third of them women. Even the secretary pops up: I Tertius, who wrote this epistle, salute you. Churches today differ on women's roles. Many Protestant churches ordain women as deacons, and some as pastors. The early churches of the East had deaconesses, and some Orthodox churches are discussing restoring them. The Catholic Church ordains only men as deacons, and has been studying the question. But every church can read this list the same way: every name was a real someone.
screen: `PHOEBE, A DIAKONOS AT CENCHREAE.` · `SHE LIKELY CARRIED THE LETTER.` · `PRISCILLA, JUNIA, RUFUS'S MOTHER.` · `I TERTIUS, WHO WROTE THIS EPISTLE.` · then, large: `I COMMEND UNTO YOU PHEBE OUR SISTER.`

segments.voice: Think of the people who keep a place of faith or care running, whose names rarely get said: the person who sets up chairs, the one who runs the food pantry, a choir director, a janitor, a nursery volunteer, a chaplain; if you don't belong to a church, anyone who serves quietly, like a school secretary, a nurse or a crossing guard. Pick one and say their name to yourself, the way Paul does: greet this one. If you pray, give thanks for them by name.
Deacon. Diakonos in Greek: a servant, a minister. And Phoebe of Cenchreae, the first name in Paul's closing list, carries it.
Your line: every name is someone. That's the end of Romans. Tomorrow, the lookout over the year.

howItsDone: Many churches remember Phoebe, Priscilla and Junia among the saints and early leaders, and in most traditions deacons serve the poor, help in worship and care for the practical life of the congregation.

original.note: Greek: servant, minister, deacon. used of Phoebe, of Paul, and of Christ.

trapdoor: what you thought: a deacon is a man who helps with the offering.
what it means: diakonos means servant or minister, and at the top of the closing list of Romans, with that title, is a woman: Phoebe.
what a scholar hears: early church writers, John Chrysostom among them, read Junia in 16:7 as a woman; later editions printed Junias, a man's name that no ancient source attests.

sources.quoted: I commend unto you Phebe our sister, which is a servant of the church which is at Cenchrea
I Tertius, who wrote this epistle, salute you

notes: Audit (10% sample): trapdoor said Junia is a woman's name 'in the earliest manuscripts'; the earliest uncials are unaccented, so the form is ambiguous there. Now it rests on early church writers (Chrysostom, Homily 31 on Romans) and the absence of 'Junias' in ancient sources. Confirm.
Phoebe as letter-carrier: widely held, not stated in the text; script says 'many scholars think'. 'The first person to read it aloud there' is a further inference; hedged with 'may have been'.
Prostatis (16:2, KJV 'succourer') rendered 'helper, a patron'; confirm.
Count of names in 16:3–15: roughly 26 people named, about 9–10 women. Script says 'more than two dozen names, and around a third of them women'. Confirm.

Phoebe is the only individual called diakonos of a specific church in Paul's letters, but Paul applies the word to himself and others (e.g. Apollos in 1 Corinthians 3:5; Tychicus in Colossians). 'First person Paul names with it' in this letter's list is accurate; in all Paul's letters, dating matters. The word segment and trapdoor now say only that she is the first name in the closing list.
Diakonos used of Christ in 15:8 (KJV 'minister'); of Paul in e.g. 2 Corinthians 3:6, Colossians 1:23. Confirm.
Church positions on women deacons: Catholic study commissions (2016, 2020); Orthodox discussion (e.g. Patriarchate of Alexandria, 2017). Confirm current state and fair wording.
Junia/Junias trapdoor: confirm the claim about manuscripts and the absence of the male name in ancient sources.
